title: Proof
body_md:
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$.
	By the definition of $K$, we have
	\(
	\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}~\text{and}~
	|x_7|=1.
	\)
	Thus $(2)$ follows immediately.

	$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$.
	Suppose that
	\(
	\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}~\text{and}~
	|x_7|=1.
	\)
	By \cite[Theorem 2.29]{apal1}, we have
	\[
	(x_i,x_{7-i},x_7)\in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
	\quad 1\leq i\leq 6.
	\]
	Since $|x_7|=1$, it follows from \cite[Theorem 7.1]{Abouhajar}
	that
	\[
	(x_i,x_{7-i},x_7)
	\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
	\quad 1\leq i\leq 6.
	\]
	By the characterization of the distinguished boundary of
	$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$, this implies
	\(
	x_i=\overline{x_{7-i}}x_7, 1\leq i\leq 6.
	\)
	Consequently, $\mathbf{x}\in K$, by the definition of $K$.

label: Lem 1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 1}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then the following
	statements hold:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item For almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$,
		\(
		x_i(z)
		=
		\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}\,x_7(z), 1\leq i\leq 6,
		\)
		and
		\[
		|x_i(z)|\leq 1,\quad 1\leq i\leq 6,
		\quad
		|x_7(z)|=1.
		\]
		
		\item The function $x_7$ is an inner function.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Since $\mathbf{x}$ is a
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function, by definition,
	\(
	\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
	\)
	for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By Proposition
	\ref{Prop K}, this is equivalent to
	\[
	\mathbf{x}(z)\in
	\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
	\quad\text{and}\quad
	|x_7(z)|=1
	\]
	for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Moreover, the  definition of $K$ give
	\(
	x_i(z)
	=
	\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}\,x_7(z), 1\leq i\leq 6,
	\)
	and
	\[
	|x_i(z)|\leq 1,
	\quad 1\leq i\leq 6.
	\]
	
	(2) Since
	\(
	x_7:\mathbb{D}\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb{D}}
	\)
	is holomorphic and its radial boundary values satisfy
	\(
	|x_7(z)|=1
	\)
	for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, it follows that $x_7$ is an
	inner function.

label: Lem 2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 2}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then
	\[
	x_i(z)
	=
	x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)\,x_7(z), \quad1\leq i\leq 6,
	\]
	for every $z\in\mathbb{C}$ for which both sides are defined.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbf{x}$ is a
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function, Lemma \ref{Lem 1} yields
	\(
	x_i(z)
	=
	\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}\,x_7(z),1\leq i\leq 6,
	\)
	for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
Recall that, for a rational function $f$, its reversed function is
	defined by
	\[
	f^\vee(z)=\overline{f(1/\overline z)}.
	\]
	Hence, for $z\in\mathbb{T}$, we have
	\[
	\overline{f(z)}
	=
	f^\vee(1/z).
	\]
	In particular,
	\[
	\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}
	=
	x_{7-i}^\vee(1/z),
	\quad z\in\mathbb{T},
	\]
	and therefore
	\[
	x_i(z)
	=
	x_{7-i}^\vee(1/z)x_7(z),
	\quad 1\leq i\leq 6,
	\]
	for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
Now, since each $x_j$ is rational, the functions
	\(
	x_i(z)~\text{and}~
	x_{7-i}^\vee(1/z)x_7(z)
	\)
	are rational functions of $z$. Their difference is therefore a
	rational function which vanishes for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
	In particular, it has infinitely many zeros with an accumulation
	point in $\mathbb{C}$ away from its poles. Hence, by the identity
	theorem for rational functions, this difference is identically zero.
	Consequently,
	\(
	x_i(z)
	=
	x_{7-i}^\vee(1/z)x_7(z),1\leq i\leq 6.
	\)
	This proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: Prop 1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop 1}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then the
	following statements hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item 
		\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $a_j\in\mathbb{C}$ be a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity
		$k_j\geq 1$, and suppose that
		$\frac{1}{\overline{a_j}}$ is a zero of $x_{7-j}$ of multiplicity
		$l_j\geq 0$. Then $a_j$ is a pole of $x_j$ of multiplicity at
		least
		\(
		k_j-l_j,
 1\leq j\leq 3,
		\)
		whenever $k_j-l_j>0$.
		\item If $\infty$ is a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity $k\geq 1$ and
		$0$ is a zero of $x_{7-j}$ of multiplicity $l_j\geq 0$, then
		$\infty$ is a pole of $x_j$ of multiplicity at least
		\(
		k-l_j, 1\leq j\leq 3,
		\)
		whenever $k-l_j>0$.
		\end{enumerate}
		
		\item \begin{enumerate}
		\item If $a_j\in\mathbb{C}$ is a pole of $x_j$ of multiplicity
		$k_j\geq 1$, then $a_j$ is a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity at
		least $k_j$, for $1\leq j\leq 3$.
	\item If $\infty$ is a pole of $x_j$ of multiplicity $k_j$, then
		$\infty$ is a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity at least
		\(
		\max\{k_1,k_2,k_3\}.
		\)
	\end{enumerate}
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: P 3
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{Lem 2}, for $1\leq i\leq 6$ we have the identity of
	rational functions
	\begin{equation}\label{P 3}
		x_i(z)=x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)x_7(z).
	\end{equation}
We first prove (1)(a). Since $x_7$ is a rational inner function on
	$\mathbb{D}$, it has no poles in $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$. Hence
	every finite pole $a_j$ of $x_7$ satisfies
	\(
	|a_j|>1.
	\)
	Consequently,
	\(
	\left|\frac{1}{a_j}\right|<1.
	\)
Fix $1\leq j\leq 3$. Suppose that $a_j$ is a pole of $x_7$ of
	multiplicity $k_j$, and that
	$\frac{1}{\overline{a_j}}$ is a zero of $x_{7-j}$ of multiplicity
	$l_j$.
Recall that
	\[
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)
	=
	\overline{x_{7-j}(1/w)}.
	\]
	Thus the zero of $x_{7-j}$ at
	$\frac{1}{\overline{a_j}}$ of multiplicity $l_j$ corresponds to a
	zero of $x_{7-j}^{\vee}$ at $a_j$ of multiplicity $l_j$. Hence
	there exists a holomorphic function $g_j$ in a neighbourhood of
	$a_j$, with
	\(
	g_j(a_j)\neq0,
	\)
	such that
	\[
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(z)
	=
	(z-a_j)^{l_j}g_j(z).
	\]
	On the other hand, since $a_j$ is a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity
	$k_j$, there exists a holomorphic function $h_j$ near $a_j$,
	with $h_j(a_j)\neq0$, such that
	\[
	x_7(z)
	=
	(z-a_j)^{-k_j}h_j(z).
	\]
	Substituting these expressions into \eqref{P 3}, we obtain
	\[
	x_j(z)
	=
	(z-a_j)^{l_j-k_j}g_j(z)h_j(z).
	\]
	Therefore, if $k_j>l_j$, then $x_j$ has a pole at $a_j$ of
	multiplicity exactly $k_j-l_j$, and in particular of multiplicity
	at least $k_j-l_j$.

	We next consider the case $(1)(b).$  Suppose that $\infty$ is a pole of $x_7$.
	Let
	\(
	w=\frac{1}{z}.
	\)
	Then $\infty$ is a pole of $x_7$ of multiplicity $k$ if and only if
	$0$ is a pole of $x_7(1/w)$ of multiplicity $k$. From
	\eqref{P 3}, with $z$ replaced by $1/w$, we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{P 4}
		x_j(1/w)
	=
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)x_7(1/w).
	\end{equation}
	
	Since $0$ is a zero of $x_{7-j}$ of multiplicity $l_j$, the
	definition of the reversed function implies that
	$x_{7-j}^{\vee}$ has a zero at $\infty$ of multiplicity $l_j$,
	or equivalently, in the local coordinate $w=1/z$, the factor
	$x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)$ has a zero at $w=0$ of multiplicity $l_j$.
	Thus
	\[
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)=w^{l_j}g_j(w),
	\qquad g_j(0)\neq0,
	\]
	while
	\[
	x_7(1/w)=w^{-k}h(w),
	\qquad h(0)\neq0.
	\]
	Consequently, \eqref{P 4} gives
	\[
	x_j(1/w)
	=
	w^{l_j-k}g_j(w)h(w).
	\]
	Therefore, if $k>l_j$, then $x_j(1/w)$ has a pole at $w=0$ of
	multiplicity $k-l_j$. Equivalently, $x_j$ has a pole at $\infty$
	of multiplicity at least $k-l_j$. This proves (1).

	We now prove (2)(a). Let $a_j\in\mathbb{C}$ be a pole of $x_j$ of
	multiplicity $k_j$. Since $x_j$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{D}$,
	we necessarily have
	\(
	|a_j|>1.
	\)
	Hence
	\(
	\left|\frac{1}{a_j}\right|<1.
	\)
	In particular, $x_{7-j}^{\vee}(1/z)$ is holomorphic and finite in a
	neighbourhood of $a_j$. More precisely, there exists a holomorphic
	function $g_j$ near $a_j$ such that
	\[
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(1/z)=g_j(z).
	\]
	By \eqref{P 3},
	\[
	x_j(z)=g_j(z)x_7(z).
	\]
	Since $x_j$ has a pole at $a_j$ of multiplicity $k_j$ while
	$g_j$ is holomorphic at $a_j$, the function $x_7$ must have a pole
	at $a_j$ of multiplicity at least $k_j$. Thus
	\[
	\operatorname{ord}_{a_j}(x_7)\leq-k_j,
	\]
	which proves the first assertion in (2)(a).

	Finally we prove $(2)(b).$  Suppose that $\infty$ is a pole of $x_j$ of multiplicity
	$k_j$. Again put $w=1/z$. Then
	$x_j(1/w)$ has a pole at $w=0$ of multiplicity $k_j$. By
	\eqref{P 4},
	\(
	x_j(1/w)
	=
	x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)x_7(1/w).
	\)
	Since $x_{7-j}$ is holomorphic at $0$, the function
	$x_{7-j}^{\vee}(w)$ is holomorphic at $w=0$. Hence the pole of
	$x_j(1/w)$ at $w=0$ must come entirely from $x_7(1/w)$.
	Therefore $x_7(1/w)$ has a pole at $w=0$ of multiplicity at least
	$k_j$. Equivalently, $x_7$ has a pole at $\infty$ of multiplicity
	at least $k_j$.
This holds for each $j=1,2,3$. Consequently, the multiplicity of
	the pole of $x_7$ at $\infty$ is at least
	\(
	\max\{k_1,k_2,k_3\}.
	\)
	This completes the proof.

label: Prop 2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop 2}
	Let
	\(
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
	=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Then the

		multiplicities $k_1,k_2\geq1$, respectively, and that
		\(
		\frac{1}{\overline{a_1}}~\text{and}~
		\frac{1}{\overline{a_2}}
		\)
		are zeros of $y_2$ and $y_1$ of multiplicities $l_1$ and $l_2$,
		respectively. Then $a_1$ and $a_2$ are poles of $x_1$ and $x_2$,
		respectively, of multiplicities at least
		\(
		k_1-l_1
		~\text{and}~
		k_2-l_2,
		\)
		whenever these quantities are positive.
		
		\item If $\infty$ is a pole of $x_3$ of multiplicity $k\geq1$ and
		$0$ is a zero of $y_2$ and $y_1$ of multiplicities $l_1$ and
		$l_2$, respectively, then $\infty$ is a pole of $x_1$ and
		$x_2$ of multiplicities at least
		\(
		k-l_1
		~\text{and}~
		k-l_2,
		\)
		respectively, whenever these quantities are positive.
		\end{enumerate}
		
		\item \begin{enumerate}
		\item If $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb{C}$ are poles of $x_1$ and $x_2$
		of multiplicities $k_1,k_2\geq1$, respectively, then $a_1$ and
		$a_2$ are poles of $x_3$ of multiplicities at least $k_1$ and
		$k_2$, respectively.
		
		\item If $\infty$ is a pole of $x_1$ and $x_2$ of multiplicities
		$k_1$ and $k_2$, respectively, then $\infty$ is a pole of
		$x_3$ of multiplicity at least
		\(
		\max\{k_1,k_2\}.
		\)\end{enumerate}
	\end{enumerate}

label: cor:reciprocal-pairing
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:reciprocal-pairing}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Suppose that
	$a\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is neither a zero nor a pole of
	$x_7$. Then, for $1\leq i\leq3$,
	\[
	\operatorname{ord}_{a}(x_i)
	=
	\operatorname{ord}_{a^*}(x_{7-i}).
	\]
	Consequently, zeros and poles of $x_i$ and $x_{7-i}$ occur in
	reciprocal-conjugate pairs and have the same multiplicities.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{Lem 2},
	\(
	x_i(z)=x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)x_7(z).
	\)
	Since $a$ is neither a zero nor a pole of $x_7$,
	\(
	\operatorname{ord}_{a}(x_7)=0.
	\)
	Taking orders at $a$ and using the reversal property gives
	\(
	\operatorname{ord}_{a}(x_i)
	=
	\operatorname{ord}_{a^*}(x_{7-i}).
	\)
	The final assertion follows immediately.
head: environment

label: cor:reciprocal-pairing-Theta
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:reciprocal-pairing-Theta}
	Let
	\(
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
	=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Suppose that
	$a\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is neither a zero nor a pole of
	$x_3$. Then
\[
	\operatorname{ord}_{a}(x_1)
	=
	\operatorname{ord}_{a^*}(y_2)\quad \text{
	and}\quad 
	\operatorname{ord}_{a}(x_2)
	=
	\operatorname{ord}_{a^*}(y_1).
	\]
	Hence the zeros and poles of $x_1$ and $y_2$, as well as those of
	$x_2$ and $y_1$, occur in reciprocal-conjugate pairs with the same
	multiplicities.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows directly from Proposition~\ref{Prop 2} and the fact
	that $a$ is neither a zero nor a pole of $x_3$. This completes the proof.

label: prop:reciprocal-orbits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:reciprocal-orbits}
	Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Suppose that $a\neq0$ is either
	a zero or a  pole of $x_i$, $1\leq i\leq3$, and that $a$ is neither a
	zero nor a pole of $x_7$. Then $a^*$ is  either a zero or a pole, respectively,
	of $x_{7-i}$ with the same multiplicity. Moreover,
	\(
	(a^*)^*=a.
	\)
In particular,  the corresponding zeros and poles occur in reciprocal pairs.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:reciprocal-pairing}.
	The second assertion follows from
	\[
	(a^*)^*
	=
	\frac{1}{\overline{1/\overline a}}
	=a.
	\] This completes the proof.

label: prop:degree-estimate
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:degree-estimate}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then
	\[
	\deg x_i
	\leq
	\deg x_{7-i}+\deg x_7,
	\quad 1\leq i\leq3.
	\]
	Similarly, if
	\(
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
	=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
	\)
	is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function, then
	\[
	\deg x_1\leq\deg y_2+\deg x_3~\text{
	and}~
	\deg x_2\leq\deg y_1+\deg x_3.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{Lem 2},
	\(
	x_i(z)=x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)x_7(z),1\leq i\leq3.
	\)
	Since reversal and the transformation $z\mapsto1/z$ preserve the
	degree of a rational function,
	\(
	\deg\big(x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)\big)=\deg x_{7-i}.
	\)
	Therefore
	\[
	\deg x_i
	\leq
	\deg x_{7-i}+\deg x_7.
	\]
	The second assertion follows similarly from Lemma~\ref{Lem 4}:
	\[
	x_1(z)=y_2^\vee(1/z)x_3(z),
	\quad
	x_2(z)=y_1^\vee(1/z)x_3(z).
	\] This completes the proof.

label: rem:fixed-points
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:fixed-points}
	The involution
	\(
	a\longmapsto a^*=\frac{1}{\overline a}
	\)
	has as its fixed-point set precisely the unit circle:
	\[
	a^*=a
	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
	|a|=1.
	\]
	Thus the reciprocal pairing described above collapses on
	$\mathbb{T}$. This is consistent with the boundary relations for
	inner functions. In particular, for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$,
	\[
	x_i(z)=\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}x_7(z),
	\quad 1\leq i\leq3,
	\]
	with $|x_7(z)|=1$, while
	\[
	x_1(z)=\overline{y_2(z)}x_3(z),
	\quad
	x_2(z)=\overline{y_1(z)}x_3(z),
	\]
	with $|x_3(z)|=1$.
Propositions~\ref{Prop 1} and~\ref{Prop 2}, together with the
	preceding corollaries, show that the components of a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function and a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function are subject to a strong
	reciprocal  structure. In particular, the map
	\(
	a\longmapsto\frac{1}{\overline a}
	\)
	provides the natural symmetry relating the corresponding component
	functions. The distinguished components $x_7$ and $x_3$ determine
	the possible deviation from an exact reciprocal correspondence.

label: Defn:degree-Gamma
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Defn:degree-Gamma}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. We define its
	degree by
	\(
		\deg(\mathbf{x}):=\deg(x_7).
	\)
	Thus, if $\deg(x_7)=n$, then
	\[
	\dim\mathcal K_{\mathbf{x}}=n+1=\deg(\mathbf{x})+1.
	\]

\label{Defn:degree-Theta}

	(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)

	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. We define its
	degree by
	\(
		\deg(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}):=\deg(x_3).
	\)
	Thus, if $\deg(x_3)=n$, then
	\[
	\dim\mathcal K_{\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}}
	=
	n+1
	=
	\deg(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})+1.
	\]
head: environment

label: Defn 3
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Defn 3}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Since
	$\mathbf{x}$ is continuous on $\mathbb T$ and
	\(
	\mathbf{x}(\mathbb T)\subseteq K,
	\)
	it induces a homomorphism
	\[
	\mathbf{x}_*:
	\pi_1(\mathbb T,1)
	\longrightarrow
	\pi_1(K,\mathbf{x}(1)).
	\]
	After identifying $\pi_1(K,\mathbf{x}(1))$ with $\mathbb Z$, we
	define the topological degree of $\mathbf{x}$ by
	\[
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})
	:=
	\mathbf{x}_*(1),
	\]
	where $1\in\mathbb Z=\pi_1(\mathbb T,1)$ denotes the standard
	generator.
head: environment

label: Lem 5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 5}
	The space $K$ is homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb T$. In particular,
	\[
	\pi_1(K)\cong\mathbb Z.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define maps
	\(
	f:K\longrightarrow\mathbb T\) by 
	\[f(x_1,\ldots,x_7)=x_7,
	\]
	and
	\(
	g:\mathbb T\longrightarrow K\) by \[
	g(\lambda)=(0,\ldots,0,\lambda).
	\]
	The map $g$ is well defined since
	\(
	(0,\ldots,0,\lambda)\in K
	~\text{for every }~\lambda\in\mathbb T.
	\)
Clearly,
	\(
	f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb T}.
	\)
On the other hand, for
$\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)\in K$ and $t\in[0,1]$, define
\[
H(\mathbf{x},t)
=
(tx_1,\ldots,tx_6,x_7).
\]
Since $\mathbf{x}\in K$, we have
\(
x_i=\overline{x_{7-i}}x_7, 1\leq i\leq6.
\)
Consequently,
\(
tx_i
=
t\overline{x_{7-i}}x_7
=
\overline{tx_{7-i}}x_7, 1\leq i\leq6,
\)
and hence
\(
H(\mathbf{x},t)\in K.
\)
Thus $H$ is a continuous map from $K\times[0,1]$ into $K$ satisfying
\[
H(\mathbf{x},0)
=
(0,\ldots,0,x_7)
=
(g\circ f)(\mathbf{x})
\]
and
\(
H(\mathbf{x},1)=\mathbf{x}.
\)
Therefore
\(
g\circ f\simeq\operatorname{id}_K.
\)
Together with
\(
f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb T},
\)
this shows that $f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses. Hence
\(
K\simeq\mathbb T.
\)
Therefore
\(
\pi_1(K)\cong\pi_1(\mathbb T)\cong\mathbb Z.
\)
head: environment

label: Prop 3
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop 3}
	Let
	\(
	\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then its
	topological degree coincides with its degree in the sense of
	Definition~\ref{Defn:degree-Gamma}. More precisely,
	\[
		\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})
		=
		\deg(\mathbf{x})
		=
		\deg(x_7).
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the map
	\[
	f:K\longrightarrow\mathbb T,
	\qquad
	f(x_1,\ldots,x_7)=x_7.
	\]
	For the rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function
	$\mathbf{x}$, we have
	\(
	f\circ\mathbf{x}=x_7
	\)
	as maps from $\mathbb T$ into $\mathbb T$.
Passing to the fundamental groups gives
	\(
	f_*\circ\mathbf{x}_*
	=
	(x_7)_*.
	\)
	By Lemma~\ref{Lem 5}, $f$ is a homotopy equivalence and hence
	\[
	f_*:\pi_1(K)\longrightarrow\pi_1(\mathbb T)
	\]
	is an isomorphism. Therefore, under the canonical identification
	of $\pi_1(K)$ with $\mathbb Z$ induced by $f$,
	\[
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})
	=
	(x_7)_*(1).
	\]
	Since $x_7$ is a finite Blaschke product,
	\(
	(x_7)_*(1)=\deg(x_7).
	\)
	Thus
	\(
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})
	=
	\deg(x_7)
	=
	\deg(\mathbf{x}).
	\)
head: environment

label: lem:K1-homotopy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:K1-homotopy}
	The set  $K_1$ of
	$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$ is homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb T$.
	In particular,
	\[
	\pi_1(K_1)\cong\mathbb Z.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
	\(
	f_1:K_1\longrightarrow\mathbb T\) by
	\[f_1(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)=x_3,
	\]
	and
	\(
	g_1:\mathbb T\longrightarrow K_1\) by 
	\[
	g_1(\lambda)=(0,0,\lambda,0,0).
	\]
	By the characterization of $K_1$ in Proposition~\ref{Prop K_1},
	$g_1$ is well defined. Clearly,
	\(
	f_1\circ g_1=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb T}.
	\)
For
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)\in K_1
\)
and $t\in[0,1]$, define
\[
H_1(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}},t)
=
(tx_1,tx_2,x_3,ty_1,ty_2).
\]
Since
\(
x_1=\overline{y_2}x_3,
x_2=\overline{y_1}x_3
\)
on $K_1$, we have
\(
tx_1=\overline{ty_2}x_3,
tx_2=\overline{ty_1}x_3.
\)
Hence
\(
H_1(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}},t)\in K_1.
\)
Moreover,
\[
H_1(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}},0)
=
(0,0,x_3,0,0)
=
(g_1\circ f_1)(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
\]
and
\(
H_1(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}},1)
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}.
\)
Thus
\(
g_1\circ f_1\simeq\operatorname{id}_{K_1}.
\)
Therefore $K_1$ is homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb T$, and hence
\(
\pi_1(K_1)\cong\mathbb Z.
\)
head: environment

label: defn:top-degree-Theta
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:top-degree-Theta}
	Let
	\(
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
	=
	(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Then
	$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ induces a homomorphism
	\[
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_*:
	\pi_1(\mathbb T,1)
	\longrightarrow
	\pi_1(K_1,\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}(1)).
	\]
	After identifying $\pi_1(K_1)$ with $\mathbb Z$ through the
	map induced by
	\[
	f_1(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)=x_3,
	\]
	we define
	\(
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
	:=
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_*(1).
	\)
head: environment

label: prop:degree-Theta
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:degree-Theta}
	Let
	\(
	\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
	=
	(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
	\)
	be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Then
	\[
		\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
	=
	\deg(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
	=
	\deg(x_3).
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition of $f_1$,
	\(
	f_1\circ\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}=x_3.
	\)
	Hence, on fundamental groups,
	\[
	(f_1)_*\circ\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_*
	=
	(x_3)_*.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:K1-homotopy}, $(f_1)_*$ is an isomorphism.
	Therefore, after identifying $\pi_1(K_1)$ with $\mathbb Z$,
	\[
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
	=
	(x_3)_*(1).
	\]
	Since $x_3$ is a finite Blaschke product,
	\(
	(x_3)_*(1)=\deg(x_3).
	\)
	Thus
	\(
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
	=
	\deg(x_3)
	=
	\deg(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}).
	\)
head: environment

label: cor:model-topological-degree
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:model-topological-degree}
	Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then
	\(
	\dim\mathcal K_{\mathbf{x}}
	=
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})+1.
	\)
	Similarly, if $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function, then
	\(
	\dim\mathcal K_{\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}}
	=
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})+1.
	\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\mathbf{x}$, Definition~\ref{Defn:degree-Gamma} and
	Proposition~\ref{Prop 3} give
	\(
	\deg(\mathbf{x})
	=
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x}).
	\)
	From the construction of $\mathcal K_{\mathbf{x}}$,
	\(
	\dim\mathcal K_{\mathbf{x}}
	=
	\deg(x_7)+1
	=
	\deg(\mathbf{x})+1.
	\)
	Hence
	\(
	\dim\mathcal K_{\mathbf{x}}
	=
	\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x})+1.
	\)
	The proof for $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is identical, using
	\(
	\dim\mathcal K_{\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}}
	=
	\deg(x_3)+1.
	\)
head: environment

label: rem:two-degree-notions
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:two-degree-notions}
	The preceding results show that the two natural notions of degree
	considered in this section coincide. For a rational
	$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function $\mathbf{x}$,
	\[
		\deg(\mathbf{x})
		=
		\deg(x_7)
		=
		\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbf{x}),
	\]
	while for a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function
	$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$,
	\[
		\deg(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})
		=
		\deg(x_3)
		=
		\deg_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}).
	\]
	Thus the degree can equivalently be interpreted analytically,
	through the associated model space, and topologically, through the
	induced homomorphism on the fundamental group.

label: Lem 8
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 8}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then, for each

label: Lem 10
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 10}
Let
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Then

(x_1,y_2,x_3)\) and \(

head: environment

label: Lem 7
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem 7}
Let
\(
\mathbf{h}=(h_1,h_2,h_3)
\)
be a triple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
$\mathbf{h}$ is a rational $\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function if and
only if, for every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(\omega h_1,\omega h_2,\omega^2h_3)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\mathbf{h}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function. Then
\(
(h_1(z),h_2(z),h_3(z))
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By \cite[Lemma 2.1]{Pal}, the
distinguished boundary $b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$ is invariant under the
transformation
\[
(a,b,c)\longmapsto
(\omega a,\omega b,\omega^2c),
\qquad \omega\in\mathbb{T}.
\]
Consequently,
\(
(\omega h_1(z),\omega h_2(z),\omega^2h_3(z))
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}
\)
for every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$ and almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
Since the transformed triple is rational and maps $\mathbb{D}$ into
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$, it is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function.

Conversely, taking $\omega=1$ gives the desired conclusion.
head: environment

label: Prop 5
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop 5}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a $7$-tuple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\item[(2)] For every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(\omega x_1,x_2,\omega x_3,\omega x_4,
\omega^2x_5,\omega x_6,\omega^2x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\item[$(2')$] For every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(\omega x_1,\omega x_2,\omega^2x_3,x_4,
\omega x_5,\omega x_6,\omega^2x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\item[$(2'')$] For every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,\omega x_2,\omega x_3,\omega x_4,
\omega x_5,\omega^2x_6,\omega^2x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove $(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)$. The proofs of
$(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2')$ and
$(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2'')$ are analogous.

Suppose that $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By \cite[Lemma 3.1]{apal2},
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\omega x_1(z),x_2(z),\omega x_3(z),\omega x_4(z),\omega^2x_5(z),\omega x_6(z),\omega^2x_7(z))
\in K
\end{aligned}
\]
for every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$ and almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
Moreover, by \cite[Lemma 2.4]{apal2},
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\omega x_1(z),x_2(z),\omega x_3(z),\omega x_4(z),\omega^2x_5(z),\omega x_6(z),\omega^2x_7(z))
\in \Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
\end{aligned}
\]
for every $z\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ and every
$\omega\in\mathbb{T}$. Hence
\(
(\omega x_1,x_2,\omega x_3,\omega x_4,
\omega^2x_5,\omega x_6,\omega^2x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

The converse follows immediately by taking $\omega=1$.
head: environment

label: Prop 6
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop 6}
Let
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
be a $5$-tuple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function if and only if, for every
$\omega\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,\omega x_2,\omega^2x_3,\omega y_1,\omega^2y_2)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. Then
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}(z)
=(x_1(z),x_2(z),x_3(z),y_1(z),y_2(z))
\in K_1
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By
\cite[Proposition 3.6]{apal2},
\[
(x_1(z),\omega x_2(z),\omega^2x_3(z),
\omega y_1(z),\omega^2y_2(z))
\in K_1
\]
for every $\omega\in\mathbb{T}$ and almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
On the other hand, by \cite[Lemma 2.8]{apal2},
\[
(x_1(z),\omega x_2(z),\omega^2x_3(z),
\omega y_1(z),\omega^2y_2(z))
\in \Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\]
for every $z\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ and every
$\omega\in\mathbb{T}$. Therefore,
\(
(x_1,\omega x_2,\omega^2x_3,\omega y_1,\omega^2y_2)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

The converse follows by taking $\omega=1$.
head: environment

label: Thm 1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm 1}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a $7$-tuple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
the following statements are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\item[(2)] $\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ and $x_7$ is inner.

\item[(3)] $\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ and at least one of the following conditions
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If
\(
|x_2(z)|<1, |x_4(z)|<1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ and $\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ are rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner functions for every
$z_2,z_3\in\mathbb{T}$.

\item[(b)] If
\(
|x_2(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_2\in\mathbb{D}$.

\item[(c)] If
\(
|x_4(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_3\in\mathbb{D}$.
\end{enumerate}

\item[(4)] $\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ and at least one of the following conditions
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If
\(
|x_1(z)|<1, |x_2(z)|<1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_1(z_1)$ and $\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ are rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner functions for every
$z_1,z_2\in\mathbb{T}$.

\item[(b)] If
\(
|x_1(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_1(z_1)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_1\in\mathbb{D}$.

\item[(c)] If
\(
|x_2(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_2\in\mathbb{D}$.
\end{enumerate}

\item[(5)] $\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ and at least one of the following conditions
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If
\(
|x_1(z)|<1,|x_4(z)|<1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_1(z_1)$ and $\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ are rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner functions for every
$z_1,z_3\in\mathbb{T}$.

\item[(b)] If
\(
|x_1(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_1(z_1)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_1\in\mathbb{D}$.

\item[(c)] If
\(
|x_4(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, then
$\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_3\in\mathbb{D}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove
\(
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)\Longleftrightarrow(3).
\)
The proofs of
\(
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)\Longleftrightarrow(4)
\)
and
\(
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)\Longleftrightarrow(5)
\)
are analogous, after the appropriate permutation of the coordinates.

The implication $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows immediately from the
definition of a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.
Conversely, suppose that
\(
\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
\)
and that $x_7$ is inner. Since
\(
|x_7(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, Proposition~\ref{Prop K} implies
that
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Hence $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Thus
\(
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2).
\)

We next prove $(1)\Rightarrow(3)$. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. By Lemma~\ref{Lem 1},
\(
x_i(z)=\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}x_7(z),1\leq i\leq6,
\)
and
\(
|x_7(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Hence
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
We consider the following three cases.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: $(1)\Rightarrow(3)(a)$:}
Suppose that
\(
|x_2(z)|<1,~|x_4(z)|<1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, and let
$z_2,z_3\in\mathbb{T}$. Then
\[
1-z_2x_2(z)\neq0,
\quad
1-z_3x_4(z)\neq0
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem 8}, the triple
$(x_2,x_5,x_7)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function. Therefore,
\[
\left|
\frac{x_5(z)-z_2x_7(z)}
     {1-z_2x_2(z)}
\right|=1, \quad z_2\in \mathbb T
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Moreover, by
\cite[Theorem 2.22]{apal1},
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1-z_2x_3}{1-z_2x_2},
\frac{x_4-z_2x_6}{1-z_2x_2},
\frac{x_5-z_2x_7}{1-z_2x_2}
\right)
\in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)} ,\quad z_2\in \mathbb T.
\]
It follows from \cite[Theorem 7.1]{Abouhajar} that
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1(z)-z_2x_3(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_4(z)-z_2x_6(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_5(z)-z_2x_7(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)}
\right)
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},\quad z_2\in \mathbb T
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Hence
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function.
Similarly, by applying Lemma~\ref{Lem 8} to the triple
$(x_4,x_3,x_7)$, we obtain that
$\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every
$z_3\in\mathbb{T}$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: $(1)\Rightarrow(3)(b)$:}
Suppose that
\(
|x_2(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, and let $z_2\in\mathbb{D}$. Then
\(
|z_2x_2(z)|<1,
\)
and hence
\(
1-z_2x_2(z)\neq0
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By Lemma~\ref{Lem 8},
\[
\left|
\frac{x_5(z)-z_2x_7(z)}
     {1-z_2x_2(z)}
\right|=1, \quad z_2\in \mathbb D
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Furthermore,
\cite[Theorem 2.29]{apal1} gives
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1-z_2x_3}{1-z_2x_2},
\frac{x_4-z_2x_6}{1-z_2x_2},
\frac{x_5-z_2x_7}{1-z_2x_2}
\right)
\in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}, \quad z_2\in \mathbb D.
\]
Therefore, its boundary values belong to
$b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb{T}$.
Consequently, $\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 3: $(1)\Rightarrow(3)(c)$:}
The proof is analogous to that of Case 2, with $x_2$ and
$\mathcal{A}_2$ replaced by $x_4$ and $\mathcal{A}_3$, respectively.
Hence $\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every $z_3\in\mathbb{D}$.
Thus,
\(
(1)\Longrightarrow(3).
\)

It remains to prove $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: $(3)(a)\Rightarrow(1)$:}
Suppose that
\(
|x_2(z)|<1, |x_4(z)|<1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, and that
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ and $\mathcal{A}_3(z_3)$ are rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner functions for every
$z_2,z_3\in\mathbb{T}$. Then, for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$,
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1(z)-z_2x_3(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_4(z)-z_2x_6(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_5(z)-z_2x_7(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)}
\right)
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}
\]
and
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1(z)-z_3x_5(z)}{1-z_3x_4(z)},
\frac{x_2(z)-z_3x_6(z)}{1-z_3x_4(z)},
\frac{x_3(z)-z_3x_7(z)}{1-z_3x_4(z)}
\right)
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}.
\]
Therefore, by \cite[Theorem 3.14]{apal1},
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Since
\(
\mathbf{x}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)},
\)
we conclude that $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: $(3)(b)\Rightarrow(1)$.}
Suppose that
\(
|x_2(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$, and that
$\mathcal{A}_2(z_2)$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}$-inner function for every $z_2\in\mathbb{D}$.
Then
\[
\left(
\frac{x_1(z)-z_2x_3(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_4(z)-z_2x_6(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)},
\frac{x_5(z)-z_2x_7(z)}{1-z_2x_2(z)}
\right)
\in b\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)}
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Hence, by
\cite[Theorem 3.14]{apal1},
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Consequently,
$\mathbf{x}$ is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 3: $(3)(c)\Rightarrow(1)$.}
The proof is analogous to that of Case 5, with $x_2$ and
$\mathcal{A}_2$ replaced by $x_4$ and $\mathcal{A}_3$, respectively.
Thus,
\(
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)\Longleftrightarrow(3).
\)
This completes
the proof.

label: Thm 4
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm 4}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a $7$-tuple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\item[(2)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_3+\eta x_5,\eta x_7,
x_2+\eta x_4,\eta x_6)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(3)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_5+\eta x_3,\eta x_7,
x_4+\eta x_2,\eta x_6)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(4)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_3+\eta x_6,\eta x_7,
x_1+\eta x_4,\eta x_5)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(5)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_6+\eta x_3,\eta x_7,
x_4+\eta x_1,\eta x_5)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(6)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_5+\eta x_6,\eta x_7,
x_1+\eta x_2,\eta x_3)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(7)] For every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_6+\eta x_5,\eta x_7,
x_2+\eta x_1,\eta x_3)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove $(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)$. The equivalences
\[
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(3),
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(4),
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(5),
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(6),~\text{and}~
(1)\Longleftrightarrow(7)
\]
follow by analogous arguments.

\medskip
\noindent
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$:
Suppose that $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Then
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)
=(x_1(z),\ldots,x_7(z))\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. By
\cite[Theorem 3.20]{apal1}, for every fixed
$\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\[
(x_1(z),x_3(z)+\eta x_5(z),\eta x_7(z),
x_2(z)+\eta x_4(z),\eta x_6(z))
\in K_1
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$.
Moreover, since
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)},
\)
\cite[Theorem 2.48]{apal1} gives
\[
(x_1(z),x_3(z)+\eta x_5(z),\eta x_7(z),
x_2(z)+\eta x_4(z),\eta x_6(z))
\in
\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\]
for every $z\in\mathbb{D}$ and every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$.
Therefore,
\(
(x_1,x_3+\eta x_5,\eta x_7,
x_2+\eta x_4,\eta x_6)
\)
is a $5$-tuple of rational functions mapping $\mathbb{D}$ into
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$ and mapping almost every point of
$\mathbb{T}$ into $K_1$. Hence it is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function for every
$\eta\in\mathbb{T}$.

\medskip
\noindent
$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$:
Suppose that, for every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$,
\(
(x_1,x_3+\eta x_5,\eta x_7,
x_2+\eta x_4,\eta x_6)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. By
Lemma~\ref{Lem 3}, for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$,
\begin{equation}\label{T 7}
x_1(z)
=
\overline{\eta x_6(z)}\,\eta x_7(z)
=
\overline{x_6(z)}x_7(z),
\quad \eta\in\mathbb{T},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{T 8}
x_3(z)+\eta x_5(z)
=
\overline{x_2(z)+\eta x_4(z)}\,\eta x_7(z),
\qquad \eta\in\mathbb{T}.
\end{equation}
Expanding the right-hand side of \eqref{T 8}, we obtain
\[
x_3(z)+\eta x_5(z)
=
\overline{x_2(z)}\,\eta x_7(z)
+
\overline{x_4(z)}\,x_7(z).
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{T 9}
x_3(z)-\overline{x_4(z)}x_7(z)
+
\eta\bigl(
x_5(z)-\overline{x_2(z)}x_7(z)
\bigr)
=0.
\end{equation}
Since \eqref{T 9} holds for every $\eta\in\mathbb{T}$, both the
constant term and the coefficient of $\eta$ must vanish. Thus,
\(
x_3(z)=\overline{x_4(z)}x_7(z)
\)
and
\(
x_5(z)=\overline{x_2(z)}x_7(z),
\)
or, equivalently,
\(
x_2(z)=\overline{x_5(z)}x_7(z),
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Together with \eqref{T 7}, we
obtain
\[
x_1(z)=\overline{x_6(z)}x_7(z),
\quad
x_2(z)=\overline{x_5(z)}x_7(z),
\quad
x_3(z)=\overline{x_4(z)}x_7(z).
\]
Furthermore, since $|\eta x_7(z)|=1$ for almost every
$z\in\mathbb{T}$, we have
\(
|x_7(z)|=1
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}. $ Therefore,
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}.$
On the other hand, by \cite[Theorem 2.48]{apal1},
the corresponding $7$-tuple maps $\mathbb{D}$ into
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$. Consequently,
$\mathbf{x}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.
This proves $(1)\Longleftrightarrow(2)$, and the proof of the theorem
is complete.

label: Thm 5
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm 5}
Let
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
be a $5$-tuple of rational functions defined on $\mathbb{D}$. Then
the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\item[(2)] The $7$-tuple
\(
\left(
x_1,\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},
\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},y_2,x_3
\right)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. By Lemma~\ref{Lem 3}, for
almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$,
\[
x_1(z)=\overline{y_2(z)}x_3(z),
\quad
x_2(z)=\overline{y_1(z)}x_3(z),
\quad
|x_3(z)|=1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x_1(z)=\overline{y_2(z)}x_3(z),\quad
\frac{y_1(z)}{2}
=
\frac{\overline{x_2(z)}}{2}x_3(z),\quad\text{
and}\quad
\frac{x_2(z)}{2}
=
\frac{\overline{y_1(z)}}{2}x_3(z)
\]
for almost every $z\in\mathbb{T}$. Together with
\(
|x_3(z)|=1,
\)
these are precisely the boundary relations required for the
$7$-tuple
\(
\left(
x_1,\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},
\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},y_2,x_3
\right)
\)
to belong to 
$K$ of $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$.
Moreover,
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbb{D})
\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}.
\)
Hence, by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{Bharali},
\[
\left(
x_1(z),\frac{y_1(z)}{2},\frac{x_2(z)}{2},
\frac{y_1(z)}{2},\frac{x_2(z)}{2},
y_2(z),x_3(z)
\right)
\in
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
\]
for every $z\in\mathbb{D}$. Therefore,
\(
\left(
x_1,\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},
\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},y_2,x_3
\right)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

Conversely, suppose that
\(
\left(
x_1,\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},
\frac{y_1}{2},\frac{x_2}{2},y_2,x_3
\right)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. The converse
implication then follows from Theorem~\ref{Thm 4}, applied to the
appropriate choice of coordinates. Hence
$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

label: Exam 1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Exam 1}
Let $\varphi,\psi\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ be two non-constant inner
functions, and let
\[
\mathbb B_3
=
\{A\in M_3(\mathbb C):\|A\|<1\}
\]
denote the open unit ball of $M_3(\mathbb C)$.

\noindent\textbf{(A)}
Consider the diagonal matrix-valued function
\[
h(z)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\varphi(z) & 0 & 0\\
0 & \psi(z) & 0\\
0 & 0 & \varphi(z)\psi(z)
\end{pmatrix},
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\]
Since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are non-constant inner functions, we have
\(
|\varphi(z)|<1, |\psi(z)|<1, z\in\mathbb D.
\)
Consequently,
\[
\|h(z)\|
=
\max\big\{
|\varphi(z)|,\,
|\psi(z)|,\,
|\varphi(z)\psi(z)|
\big\}
<1,
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\]
Thus, $h:\mathbb D\to\mathbb B_3$ is holomorphic. Define
\(
\mathbf{x}
=
\Pi_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}\circ h.
\)
By \cite[Theorem 2.41]{apal1}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{x}(z)
={}
\big(
\varphi(z),\,
\psi(z),\,
\varphi(z)\psi(z),\,
\varphi(z)\psi(z),\,
\varphi^2(z)\psi(z),
\varphi(z)\psi^2(z),\,
\varphi^2(z)\psi^2(z)
\big)
\in
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)},
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, $\mathbf{x}$ is a holomorphic map from $\mathbb D$ into
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$. Since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are inner
functions, their radial boundary values are unimodular almost
everywhere on $\mathbb T$. Therefore,
\[
|x_7(\zeta)|
=
|\varphi(\zeta)|^2|\psi(\zeta)|^2
=1
\]
for almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$. Moreover, for almost every
$\zeta\in\mathbb T$,
\[
x_i(\zeta)
=
\overline{x_{7-i}(\zeta)}\,x_7(\zeta),
\quad 1\leq i\leq6.
\]
Thus $\mathbf{x}(\zeta)\in K$ for almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$.
Hence $\mathbf{x}$ is a $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{(B)}
The preceding example can be generalized by applying unitary
transformations to the matrix-valued function $h$. Consider the
unitary matrices
\[
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\\
0 & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
V=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Define
\[
g(z)=Uh(z)V,\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\]
Since $U$ and $V$ are unitary, we have
\[
\|g(z)\|=\|h(z)\|<1,
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\]
Therefore, $g:\mathbb D\to\mathbb B_3$ is holomorphic. Explicitly,
\[
g(z)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\varphi(z) & 0 & 0\\[1mm]
0 & \dfrac{\psi(z)}{\sqrt2}
  & \dfrac{\varphi(z)\psi(z)}{\sqrt2}\\[2mm]
0 & -\dfrac{\psi(z)}{\sqrt2}
  & \dfrac{\varphi(z)\psi(z)}{\sqrt2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}
=
\Pi_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}\circ g.
\)
Then, by \cite[Theorem 2.41]{apal1},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{x}(z)
=
\Big(
\varphi(z),\,
\dfrac{\psi(z)}{\sqrt2},\,
\dfrac{\varphi(z)\psi(z)}{\sqrt2},\,
\dfrac{\varphi(z)\psi(z)}{\sqrt2},\dfrac{\varphi^2(z)\psi(z)}{\sqrt2},\,
\varphi(z)\psi^2(z),\,
\varphi^2(z)\psi^2(z)
\Big),
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular,
\(
\mathbf{x}(\mathbb D)
\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}.
\)
Furthermore, since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are inner functions, the
radial boundary values of $\mathbf{x}$ satisfy
\(
|x_7(\zeta)|=1
\)
for almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, and the defining relations of
 $K$ are satisfied almost everywhere.
Consequently,
\[
\mathbf{x}(\zeta)\in K
\]
for almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$. Hence $\mathbf{x}$ is a
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function.

\medskip
In Example~\ref{Exam 1}(A), the coordinates satisfy the relations
\begin{equation}\label{E 1}
\begin{aligned}
x_1x_2 =x_3,
x_1x_4 =x_5,
x_2x_4 =x_6,
x_1x_6 =x_7,
x_2x_5= x_7,
x_3x_4 =x_7,
\end{aligned}
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\end{equation}
These identities illustrate the multiplicative structure underlying
this particular example.

label: Exam 2
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Exam 2}
Let $\varphi,\psi$ and $\mathbb B_3$ be as in
Example~\ref{Exam 1}.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{(A)}
From Example~\ref{Exam 1}(A), the function
\(
\mathbf{x}
=
\big(
\varphi,\,
\psi,\,
\varphi\psi,\,
\varphi\psi,\,
\varphi^2\psi,\,
\varphi\psi^2,\,
\varphi^2\psi^2
\big)
\)
is a $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Hence, by
Theorem~\ref{Thm 4}, for every fixed $\eta\in\mathbb T$, the function
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_\eta
=
\big(
x_1,\,
x_3+\eta x_5,\,
\eta x_7,\,
x_2+\eta x_4,\,
\eta x_6
\big)
\]
is a $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. In the present case, this
gives
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_\eta
=
\big(
\varphi,\,
\varphi\psi+\eta\varphi^2\psi,\,
\eta\varphi^2\psi^2,\,
\psi+\eta\varphi\psi,\,
\eta\varphi\psi^2
\big).
\]
Thus, for every $\eta\in\mathbb T$,
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_\eta
=
\big(
\varphi,\,
\varphi\psi(1+\eta\varphi),\,
\eta\varphi^2\psi^2,\,
\psi(1+\eta\varphi),\,
\eta\varphi\psi^2
\big)
\)
is a $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{(B)}
Similarly, starting from the
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function constructed in
Example~\ref{Exam 1}(B), Theorem~\ref{Thm 4} yields further examples
of $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner functions. For instance, using the
transformation
\[
\big(
x_1,\,
x_3+\eta x_5,\,
\eta x_7,\,
x_2+\eta x_4,\,
\eta x_6
\big),
\quad \eta\in\mathbb T,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_\eta
=
\Big(
\varphi,\,
\dfrac{\varphi\psi}{\sqrt2}
+\eta\dfrac{\varphi^2\psi}{\sqrt2},\,
\eta\varphi^2\psi^2,\psi/\sqrt2
+\eta\varphi\psi/\sqrt2,\,
\eta\varphi\psi^2
\Big).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_\eta$ is a
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function for every $\eta\in\mathbb T$.
head: environment

label: Description 1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Description 1}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function of degree $n$.
Then there exist polynomials
\(
E_1,\ldots,E_6,D
\)
such that the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \(
    \deg E_i\leq n,1\leq i\leq6,
    \deg D\leq n.
    \)

    \item
    \(
    D(z)\neq0, z\in\overline{\mathbb D}.
    \)

    \item
    \(
    x_i=\frac{E_i}{D}, 1\leq i\leq6,
    x_7=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}
    \)
    on $\overline{\mathbb D}$.

    \item
    \(
    |E_i(z)|\leq |D(z)|,
     z\in\overline{\mathbb D},
    1\leq i\leq6.
    \)

    \item
    \(
    E_i=E_{7-i}^{\sim n},
    1\leq i\leq6.
    \)
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if
\(
\{E'_1,\ldots,E'_6,D'\}
\)
is another collection of polynomials satisfying $(1)$--$(5)$ and
representing the same function $\mathbf{x}$, then there exists
$t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ such that
\[
D'=tD,
\quad
E'_i=tE_i, \quad1\leq i\leq6.
\]
Conversely, every such real non-zero scalar multiple also satisfies
$(1)$--$(5)$ and represents the same function $\mathbf{x}$.
head: environment

label: x_7
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function of degree $n$.
By Lemma~\ref{Lem 1}, $x_7$ is a rational inner function of degree
$n$. Therefore, by the representation
\eqref{Description of inner function}, there exists a polynomial $D$
of degree at most $n$ such that
\(
D(z)\neq0, z\in\overline{\mathbb D},
\)
and
\begin{equation}\label{x_7}
x_7=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}.
\end{equation}
Since $\deg(x_7)=n$, Proposition~\ref{Prop 1}(2) implies that every
pole of $x_i$, $1\leq i\leq6$, is also a pole of $x_7$, with
multiplicity no greater than the corresponding multiplicity of the
pole of $x_7$. Hence, for each $1\leq i\leq6$, there exists a
polynomial $E_i$ with $\deg E_i\leq n$ such that
\(
x_i=\frac{E_i}{D}.
\)
Since
\(
\mathbf{x}(\mathbb D)
\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)},
\)
we have
\[
|x_i(z)|\leq1,
\quad z\in\mathbb D,
\quad 1\leq i\leq6.
\]
By continuity, the same inequality holds on
$\overline{\mathbb D}$. Consequently,
\[
|E_i(z)|\leq |D(z)|,
\quad z\in\overline{\mathbb D},
\quad 1\leq i\leq6.
\]
This proves $(1)$--$(4)$.

It remains to establish $(5)$. By Lemma~\ref{Lem 2}, for almost every
$z\in\mathbb T$,
\begin{equation}\label{Des 1}
x_i(z)
=
x_{7-i}^{\vee}(1/z)x_7(z),
\quad 1\leq i\leq6.
\end{equation}
Using \eqref{x_7}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{Des 2}
\frac{E_i(z)}{D(z)}
=
\frac{\overline{E_{7-i}(1/\overline z)}}
     {\overline{D(1/\overline z)}}
\frac{z^n\overline{D(1/\overline z)}}{D(z)}
\end{equation}
for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$. Hence
\[
E_i(z)
=
z^n\overline{E_{7-i}(1/\overline z)}
=
E_{7-i}^{\sim n}(z),
\quad z\in\mathbb T.
\]
Since both sides are polynomials, the identity theorem yields
\(
E_i=E_{7-i}^{\sim n},
 1\leq i\leq6.
\)
Thus $(5)$ holds.
We now prove the uniqueness assertion. Let
\(
\{E'_1,\ldots,E'_6,D'\}
\)
be another collection of polynomials satisfying $(1)$--$(5)$ and
representing the same function $\mathbf{x}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{Des 4}
\frac{E_i}{D}
=
\frac{E'_i}{D'},
\quad 1\leq i\leq6,
\quad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}
=
\frac{D'^{\sim n}}{D'}.
\end{equation}
Since $D$ and $D'$ have no zeros in $\overline{\mathbb D}$ and
represent the same rational inner function $x_7$, they have the same
zeros in $\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$, counted with
multiplicity. Hence there exists $t\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ such
that
\(
D'=tD.
\)
Substituting this into the second equality in \eqref{Des 4}, we get
\(
\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}
=
\frac{\overline{t}\,D^{\sim n}}{tD}.
\)
Therefore $\overline t=t$, and hence
\(
t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\)
Finally, the first equality in \eqref{Des 4} gives
\(
\frac{E_i}{D}
=
\frac{E'_i}{tD},
\)
and consequently
\(
E'_i=tE_i,
 1\leq i\leq6.
\)
The converse is immediate: if
\[
D'=tD,\quad E'_i=tE_i,
\quad t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},
\]
then $(1)$--$(5)$ remain valid and the resulting rational functions
are unchanged. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: Rem 2
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem 2}
Let
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. By
Lemma~\ref{Lem 1}, for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$,
\[
x_i(z)=\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}x_7(z),
\quad 1\leq i\leq6,\quad \text{
and}\quad
|x_7(z)|=1.
\]
Consequently,
\(
|x_i(z)|=|x_{7-i}(z)|, 1\leq i\leq6,
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$.

label: Partial Converse 1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Partial Converse 1}
Let $E_1,\ldots,E_6,D$ be polynomials satisfying conditions
$(1)$, $(2)$, $(4)$, and $(5)$ of Theorem~\ref{Description 1}.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{x_i, x_7}
x_i=\frac{E_i}{D},
\quad 1\leq i\leq6,
\quad
x_7=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}.
\end{equation}
Suppose that at least one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \(
    (x_2(z),x_4(z),x_6(z))
    \in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
     z\in\mathbb T;
    \)

    \item
    \(
    (x_1(z),x_4(z),x_5(z))
    \in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
    z\in\mathbb T;
    \)

    \item
    \(
    (x_1(z),x_2(z),x_3(z))
    \in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
     z\in\mathbb T.
    \)
\end{enumerate}
Then
\(
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
is a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function of degree at
most $n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, assume that
\(
(x_2(z),x_4(z),x_6(z))
\in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
 z\in\mathbb T.
\)
We divide the proof into three steps.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Step 1: $x_7$ is rational inner.}
Since $D$ has no zeros in $\overline{\mathbb D}$, the function
\[
x_7=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}
\]
is a rational inner function. If $D$ and $D^{\sim n}$ have common
zeros on $\mathbb T$, the corresponding common factors may cancel.
Therefore,
\(
\deg(x_7)\leq n.
\)

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Step 2: $\mathbf{x}$ has boundary values in $K$.}
By condition $(5)$ of Theorem~\ref{Description 1},
\(
E_i=E_{7-i}^{\sim n},
1\leq i\leq6.
\)
Consequently, by the same calculation as in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{Description 1},
\(
x_i(z)
=
\overline{x_{7-i}(z)}x_7(z),
1\leq i\leq6,
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$. Since $|x_7(z)|=1$ almost
everywhere on $\mathbb T$, it follows from
\cite[Theorem 3.14]{apal1} that
\(
\mathbf{x}(z)\in K
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb T.$

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Step 3: $\mathbf{x}$ maps $\mathbb D$ into
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$.}
By \cite[Theorem 2.39]{apal1}, it suffices to prove
\begin{equation}\label{Con Des 2}
\|\Psi^{(1)}(\cdot,\mathbf{x}(z))\|_{H^\infty(\mathbb D^2)}
\leq1,
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\end{equation}
Since
\(
\mathbf{x}(\zeta)\in K
\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
\)
for almost every $\zeta\in\mathbb T$, 
\cite[ Theorem~2.39]{apal1} gives
\[
|\Psi^{(1)}(z_2,z_3,\mathbf{x}(\zeta))|
\leq1
\]
for every fixed $z_2,z_3\in\overline{\mathbb D}$ and for almost every
$\zeta\in\mathbb T$.
Fix $z_2,z_3\in\overline{\mathbb D}$. Since
\(
(x_2(\zeta),x_4(\zeta),x_6(\zeta))
\in\Gamma_{E(2;2;1,1)},
 \zeta\in\mathbb T,
\)
the denominator of
\(
\Psi^{(1)}(z_2,z_3,\mathbf{x}(\zeta))
\)
does not vanish for $\zeta\in\mathbb T$. Since each $x_i$ is
holomorphic on $\mathbb D$, the function
\[
z\longmapsto
\Psi^{(1)}(z_2,z_3,\mathbf{x}(z))
\]
is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$. The maximum modulus principle
therefore yields
\[
|\Psi^{(1)}(z_2,z_3,\mathbf{x}(z))|
\leq1,
\quad z\in\mathbb D.
\]
Since $z_2,z_3\in\overline{\mathbb D}$ were arbitrary,
\eqref{Con Des 2} follows. Hence
\(
\mathbf{x}(\mathbb D)
\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}.
\)
Thus $\mathbf{x}$ is a rational map from $\mathbb D$ into
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ whose radial boundary values belong to $K$
almost everywhere on $\mathbb T$. Therefore $\mathbf{x}$ is a
rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function. Its degree is
$\deg(x_7)\leq n$. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: Rem 3
title: Remark

label: Description 2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Description 2}
Let
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=
(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function of degree $n$.
Then there exist polynomials
\(
E_1,E_2,F_1,F_2,D
\)
such that the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \(
    \deg E_i\leq n,
    \deg F_i\leq n,
     1\leq i\leq2,
    \deg D\leq n.
    \)

    \item
    \(
    D(z)\neq0,
     z\in\overline{\mathbb D}.
    \)

    \item
    \(
    x_i=\frac{E_i}{D},
    y_i=\frac{F_i}{D}, 1\leq i\leq2,
    x_3=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D}
    \)
    on $\overline{\mathbb D}$.

    \item
    \(
    |E_1(z)|\leq|D(z)|,
    |E_2(z)|\leq2|D(z)|,
    |F_1(z)|\leq2|D(z)|,
    |F_2(z)|\leq|D(z)|,
    \)
    for all $z\in\overline{\mathbb D}$.

    \item
    \(
    E_i=F_{3-i}^{\sim n},
    1\leq i\leq2.
    \)
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if
\(
\{E'_1,E'_2,F'_1,F'_2,D'\}
\)
is another collection of polynomials satisfying $(1)$--$(5)$ and
representing the same function
$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$, then there exists
$t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ such that
\[
D'=tD,
\quad
E'_i=tE_i,
\quad
F'_i=tF_i,
\quad 1\leq i\leq2.
\]
Conversely, every such real non-zero scalar multiple also satisfies
$(1)$--$(5)$ and represents the same function
$\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is analogous to that of Theorem~\ref{Description 1}. By
Lemma~\ref{Lem 3}, $x_3$ is a rational inner function of degree $n$.
Hence, by \eqref{Description of inner function},
\(
x_3=\frac{D^{\sim n}}{D},
\)
where $D$ has degree at most $n$ and has no zeros in
$\overline{\mathbb D}$.
By the pole relations for the components of a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function, each of $x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2$
has poles contained among those of $x_3$, with no larger
multiplicities. Consequently, there exist polynomials
$E_1,E_2,F_1,F_2$ of degree at most $n$ such that
\[
x_i=\frac{E_i}{D},
\quad
y_i=\frac{F_i}{D},
\quad 1\leq i\leq2.
\]
The bounds in $(4)$ follow from
\[
|x_1|\leq1,\quad
|x_2|\leq2,\quad
|y_1|\leq2,\quad
|y_2|\leq1
\]
on $\overline{\mathbb D}$.
Finally, Lemma~\ref{Lem 3} gives, almost everywhere on $\mathbb T$,
\[
x_1=\overline{y_2}\,x_3,
\quad
x_2=\overline{y_1}\,x_3,
\quad
|x_3|=1.
\]
Substituting the polynomial representations and using the
representation of $x_3$ gives
\[
E_1=F_2^{\sim n},
\qquad
E_2=F_1^{\sim n}.
\]
Thus $(5)$ holds.
The uniqueness assertion follows exactly as in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{Description 1}. Indeed, two denominators representing
the same rational inner function $x_3$ differ by a non-zero scalar.
The self-inversive relation in $(5)$ forces this scalar to be real,
and the representations of $x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2$ then imply the
corresponding scalar relations for $E_i$ and $F_i$.
head: environment

label: Rem 4
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem 4}
Let
\(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=
(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
be a rational $\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function. By
Lemma~\ref{Lem 3}, for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$,
\[
x_1(z)=\overline{y_2(z)}x_3(z),
\quad
x_2(z)=\overline{y_1(z)}x_3(z),
\quad
|x_3(z)|=1.
\]
Consequently,
\(
|x_1(z)|=|y_2(z)|,
|x_2(z)|=|y_1(z)|
\)
for almost every $z\in\mathbb T$.

label: Partial Converse 2
title: Theorem
body_md:

$(1)$, $(2)$, $(4)$, and $(5)$ of Theorem~\ref{Description 2}.
Define

\quad

label: Interpolation in M_n(C)
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Interpolation in M_n(C)}
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be distinct points in $\mathbb D$, and let
$W_1,\ldots,W_m\in M_n(\mathbb C)$. Then there exists a matrix-valued
Schur function
\(
F:\mathbb D\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb C)
\)
such that
\[
F(z_j)=W_j,\quad 1\leq j\leq m,
\]
if and only if the block Pick matrix
\[
\left(
\frac{I_n-W_iW_j^*}{1-z_i\overline{z}_j}
\right)_{i,j=1}^{m}
\]
is positive semidefinite.

label: Inter
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Inter}
Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfy
\[
r(W_j)<1,\quad 1\leq j\leq m,
\]
where $r(\cdot)$ denotes the spectral radius. Then there exists a
holomorphic function
\(
G:\mathbb D\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb C)
\)
such that
\(
\sup_{z\in\mathbb D}\|G(z)\|<1
\)
and
\(
G(z_j)=X_jW_jX_j^{-1},
1\leq j\leq m,
\)
for some invertible matrices $X_1,\ldots,X_m\in M_n(\mathbb C)$.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $a,b\in\mathbb D$. By the Schwarz-type characterization of
$G_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$ (see \cite[Theorem 2.22]{apal1}), the function
\(
\Psi_{a,b}^{(1)}
\)
maps $G_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$ into $\mathbb D$. Hence
\(
F_{a,b}(z)
=
\Psi_{a,b}^{(1)}(h(z))
\)
belongs to the scalar Schur class. Since
\(
F_{a,b}(z_j)
=
\Psi_{a,b}^{(1)}(h(z_j)),
\)
the classical Nevanlinna--Pick theorem yields
\[
\left(
\frac{
1-\overline{F_{a,b}(z_j)}F_{a,b}(z_i)
}{
1-\overline{z_j}z_i
}
\right)_{i,j=1}^{N}
\geq0.
\]
Substituting the definition of $F_{a,b}$ gives the asserted
positivity.
The assertions concerning $\Psi_{a,b}^{(2)}$ and
$\Psi_{a,b}^{(3)}$ follow in exactly the same manner.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Interpolation in G_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}}
Let
\(
z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb D
\)
be distinct points, and let
\[
\mathbf{x}_j=(x_{1j},\dots,x_{7j})
\in
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr),\quad
1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Suppose that there exists a holomorphic function
\[
h:\mathbb D\longrightarrow
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr)
\]
such that
\(
h(z_j)=\mathbf{x}_j,
1\leq j\leq N.
\)
Then there exists a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$-inner function
\[
\widetilde h:\mathbb D\longrightarrow
\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}
\]
such that
\(
\widetilde h(z_j)=\mathbf{x}_j,
1\leq j\leq N.
\) 

Moreover, the rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function
$\widetilde h$ admits the following explicit representation. There
exist $n\in\mathbb N$, $\xi\in\mathbb T$, and
$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\in\mathbb D$ such that, for each
$1\leq k\leq3$, there exist
\(
t_k,q_k\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\},
r_k\in\mathbb R,
\)
and
\(
\eta_k,\delta_k,\xi_{k,1},\ldots,\xi_{k,t_k}\in\mathbb T,
\beta_{k,1},\ldots,\beta_{k,q_k}\in\mathbb D,
\)
satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{*}
t_k+q_k=n,
\quad
\eta_k\delta_k
\prod_{i=1}^{t_k}\xi_{k,i}
=\xi.
\end{equation}
Then
\(
\widetilde h=(x_1,\ldots,x_7),
\)
where
\begin{equation}\label{x_7 Representation}
x_7(z)
=
\xi\prod_{i=1}^n
\frac{z-\alpha_i}
     {1-\overline{\alpha_i}z},
\end{equation}
and, for $1\leq k\leq3$,
\begin{equation}\label{x_k_x_7-k_Representation}
\begin{aligned}
x_k(z)
=
r_k\eta_k
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_k}(\xi_{k,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_k}f_{k,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
},\quad
x_{7-k}(z)
=
r_k\delta_k
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_k}(\xi_{k,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_k}g_{k,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where, for each $1\leq i\leq q_k$, either
\(
f_{k,i}(z)=\overline{\beta}_{k,i}z-1,
g_{k,i}(z)=\beta_{k,i}-z,
\)
or
\(
f_{k,i}(z)=\beta_{k,i}-z,
g_{k,i}(z)=\overline{\beta}_{k,i}z-1.
\)
In particular, for $z\in\mathbb T$, the factors in
\eqref{x_k_x_7-k_Representation}, together with condition \eqref{*},
give
\(
x_k(z)
=
\overline{x_{7-k}(z)}\,x_7(z),
 1\leq k\leq3.
\)
Moreover,
\(
|x_7(z)|=1, z\in\mathbb T.
\)
Consequently,
\(
\widetilde h(\mathbb T)\subseteq K.
\)
Thus $\widetilde h$ is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner function whose boundary values lie in
$K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M$ be a holomorphic lifting associated with
$\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$, so that
\[
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}\circ M=\operatorname{id}
\]
on the relevant domain and
\(
M\circ h:\mathbb D\longrightarrow B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1).
\)
Put
\(
f=M\circ h.
\)
Then
\(
\|f(z)\|<1, z\in\mathbb D.
\)
In particular,
\(
r(f(z))<1, z\in\mathbb D.
\)
For $0<\varepsilon<1$, define
\(
f_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon f(z).
\)
Then
\(
r(f_\varepsilon(z))<1,z\in\mathbb D.
\)
By Theorem~\ref{Inter}, there exists a holomorphic function
\[
F_\varepsilon:\mathbb D\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb C)
\]
such that
\(
\sup_{z\in\mathbb D}\|F_\varepsilon(z)\|<1
\)
and
\(
F_\varepsilon(z_j)
\sim
\varepsilon f(z_j),
1\leq j\leq N.
\)
Here $\sim$ denotes similarity.
Since the family $\{F_\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon<1\}$ is locally bounded,
Montel's theorem yields a sequence
$\varepsilon_\nu\to1$ such that
\(
F_{\varepsilon_\nu}\longrightarrow F
\)
locally uniformly on $\mathbb D$, where
\(
F:\mathbb D\longrightarrow
\overline{B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)}.
\)
Moreover, the similarity relation at the interpolation nodes implies
\[
\sigma(F(z_j))
=
\sigma(f(z_j)),
\quad
1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Since $\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$ depends only on the spectral data,
we obtain
\[
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}(F(z_j))
=
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}(f(z_j))
=
h(z_j).
\]
By the matrix-valued Nevanlinna--Pick interpolation theorem, there
exists a rational matrix inner function
\(
F_0:\mathbb D\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb C)
\)
which interpolates the same spectral data at the points $z_j$.
Thus,
\[
F_0(z_j)\sim f(z_j),
\quad
1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Define
\(
\widetilde h
=
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}\circ F_0.
\)
Since $F_0$ is rational inner, its radial boundary values are unitary
almost everywhere on $\mathbb T$. Consequently, the corresponding
spectral data belong to 
\(
K\subseteq
\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}
\)
almost everywhere on $\mathbb T$. Hence
\(
\widetilde h
\)
is a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$-inner function.
Finally, at each interpolation node,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde h(z_j)
&=
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}(F_0(z_j))\\
&=
\Pi_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}(f(z_j))\\
&=
h(z_j)\\
&=
\mathbf{x}_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
We now record the rational representation of the interpolating
function. Let
\(
\widetilde h
=
(x_1,\ldots,x_7)
\)
be a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$-inner function. Since
$x_7$ is a scalar rational inner function, it is a finite Blaschke
product. Thus
\[
x_7(z)
=
\xi
\prod_{j=1}^{N}
\frac{z-\alpha_j}{1-\overline{\alpha_j}z},
\quad
|\xi|=1,\quad
\alpha_j\in\mathbb D.
\]
The boundary relations for
$\Gamma_{E(3;3,1,1,1)}$ give
\[
x_k(\zeta)
=
\overline{x_{7-k}(\zeta)}\,x_7(\zeta),
\quad
\zeta\in\mathbb T,
\quad
1\leq k\leq3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{x_k(\zeta)x_{7-k}(\zeta)}
{x_7(\zeta)}
=
|x_{7-k}(\zeta)|^2,
\quad
\zeta\in\mathbb T.
\]
The function on the left-hand side is rational and nonnegative on
$\mathbb T$. By the standard factorization theorem for nonnegative
rational functions on the unit circle (see \cite[p.~137]{Duren}), it
admits a factorization into finite Blaschke factors.
More precisely, for each $1\leq k\leq3$, there exist integers
$t_k,q_k\geq0$ with
\(
t_k+q_k=N,
\)
constants
\(
r_k>0,
|\eta_k|=|\delta_k|=1,
|\xi_{k,j}|=1,
\)
and finite Blaschke factors $f_{k,j}$ and $g_{k,j}$ such that
\[
x_k(z)
=
r_k\eta_k
\frac{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=1}^{t_k}(\xi_{k,j}+z)
\prod_{j=1}^{q_k}f_{k,j}(z)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1-\overline{\alpha_j}z)
},\quad \text{
and}\quad
x_{7-k}(z)
=
r_k\delta_k
\frac{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=1}^{t_k}(\xi_{k,j}+z)
\prod_{j=1}^{q_k}g_{k,j}(z)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1-\overline{\alpha_j}z)
}.
\]
The factors may be chosen in either of the two forms
\[
f_{k,j}(z)
=
\overline{\beta_{k,j}}z-1,
\qquad
g_{k,j}(z)
=
\beta_{k,j}-z,
\]
or
\[
f_{k,j}(z)
=
\beta_{k,j}-z,
\qquad
g_{k,j}(z)
=
\overline{\beta_{k,j}}z-1,
\]
where
\(
|\beta_{k,j}|=1.
\)
The unimodular constants satisfy the compatibility condition
\[
\eta_k\delta_k
\prod_{j=1}^{t_k}\xi_{k,j}
=
\xi.
\]
This proves the result.

label: Interpolation 2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Interpolation 2}
Let $w_1,\ldots,w_N\in\mathbb D$ be distinct points, and let
\[
(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j})
\in G_{E(3;2;1,2)},
\quad 1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Suppose that there exists a holomorphic map
\(
h:\mathbb D\longrightarrow G_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\)
such that
\[
h(w_j)
=
(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j}),
\quad 1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Then, for every fixed $z\in\mathbb D$, the Pick matrix
\[
\left(
\frac{1-\overline{\widetilde w_j}\widetilde w_i}
     {1-\overline{w_j}w_i}
\right)_{i,j=1}^{N}
\]
is positive semidefinite, where
\(
\widetilde w_j
=
\Psi_3
\bigl(
z,(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j})
\bigr),
1\leq j\leq N,
\)
and
\(
(y_{1,j},y_{2,j})\in G_{E(2;1;2)}.
\)

label: parameters E3212
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Interpolation in G_{E(3;2;1,2)}}
Let $w_1,\ldots,w_N\in\mathbb D$ be distinct points and suppose that
\[
(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j})
\in
\Pi_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr),
\quad 1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Suppose further that there exists a holomorphic map
\(
h:\mathbb D\longrightarrow G_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\)
such that
\[
h(w_j)
=
(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j}),
\quad 1\leq j\leq N,
\]
and
\(
h(\mathbb D)
\subseteq
\Pi_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr).
\)
Then there exists a rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function
\(
\widetilde h:\mathbb D
\longrightarrow
\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\)
such that
\[
\widetilde h(w_j)
=
(x_{1,j},x_{2,j},x_{3,j},y_{1,j},y_{2,j}),
\quad 1\leq j\leq N.
\]
Furthermore, $\widetilde h$ admits the following explicit
representation. There exist $n\in\mathbb N$, $\xi\in\mathbb T$, and
$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\in\mathbb D$ such that, for each
$k=1,2$, there exist
\(
t_k,q_k\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\},
r_k\in\mathbb R,
\)
and
\(
\eta_k,\delta_k,\xi_{k,1},\ldots,\xi_{k,t_k}\in\mathbb T,
\beta_{k,1},\ldots,\beta_{k,q_k}\in\mathbb D,
\)
satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{parameters E3212}
t_k+q_k=n,
\qquad
\eta_k\delta_k
\prod_{i=1}^{t_k}\xi_{k,i}
=
\xi,
\qquad k=1,2.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
x_3(z)
=
\xi
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{z-\alpha_i}
     {1-\overline{\alpha_i}z},
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{x_1_x_2_y_1_y_2 Representation}
\begin{aligned}
&x_1(z)
=
r_1\eta_1
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_1}(\xi_{1,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_1}f_{1,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
},\quad
x_2(z)
=
r_2\eta_2
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_2}(\xi_{2,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_2}f_{2,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
},
\\[2mm]
&y_1(z)
=
r_2\delta_2
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_2}(\xi_{2,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_2}g_{2,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
},\quad
y_2(z)
=
r_1\delta_1
\frac{
\displaystyle
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t_1}(\xi_{1,i}+z)\right)
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q_1}g_{1,i}(z)\right)
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\overline{\alpha_i}z-1)
}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here, for each $1\leq i\leq q_k$, either
\(
f_{k,i}(z)=\overline{\beta}_{k,i}z-1,
g_{k,i}(z)=\beta_{k,i}-z,
\)
or
\(
f_{k,i}(z)=\beta_{k,i}-z,
g_{k,i}(z)=\overline{\beta}_{k,i}z-1.
\)
The rational map
\(
\widetilde h
=
(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2)
\)
is the required rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner function interpolating the prescribed
data.

label: Rem 5
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem 5}
The results obtained in this section provide a partial solution to
the interpolation problem by rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner and
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner functions. More precisely, we construct
rational $\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner functions and rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner functions interpolating prescribed data
whenever the corresponding interpolation points belong to
\[
\Pi_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr)\quad \text{
and}\quad
\Pi_{E(3;2;1,2)}
\bigl(B_{M_3(\mathbb C)}(0,1)\bigr),
\]
respectively. Thus, the general interpolation problem by rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$-inner and rational
$\Gamma_{E(3;2;1,2)}$-inner functions for arbitrary interpolation
points in
$G_{E(3;3;1,1,1)}$ and
$G_{E(3;2;1,2)}$, respectively, remains open.
